prompt: Three independent voters are each right 80% of the time. What is the probability that their majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hint: All three right, plus exactly two right.

prompt: Three independent voters are each right 40% of the time. How does their majority compare with one of them?
hint: Work out the same sum at 0.4.

choices.text: Better, as with any vote
choices.why: The gain only appears above one half.

choices.text: Exactly the same
choices.why: That would need the three to make the same mistakes.

choices.text: Worse: 0.352 against 0.4
choices.why: Right: a majority of voters who are usually wrong is wrong more reliably.

choices.text: It cannot be computed without knowing which voter is the best of the three
choices.why: All three have the same accuracy here; the sum needs nothing else.

prompt: The 0.896 for three voters at 80% depends on one assumption. Which?
hint: It is what lets you multiply the error rates.

choices.text: That the voters are prompts rather than models
choices.why: The arithmetic does not care what a voter is.

choices.text: That one voter's mistakes make no other's more likely
choices.why: Right: independence, which is what lets 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04.

choices.text: That ties are settled by the first voter
choices.why: With two labels and three voters there is no tie to settle.

choices.text: That every voter runs at temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature is not in the sum.

prompt: Three independent voters are each right 70% of the time. What is the probability that their majority is right? Give it as a decimal.
hint: 0.7 cubed, plus three times 0.7 squared times 0.3.

prompt: Three voters at 80% make exactly the same mistakes on exactly the same messages. How often is their majority right?
hint: When one is wrong, so are the others.

choices.text: 80% of the time, the same as any one of them
choices.why: Right: three copies of one voter are one voter.

choices.text: 89.6% of the time
choices.why: That needs independent mistakes.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: They are right together 80% of the time.

choices.text: 51.2% of the time, since all three must be right together
choices.why: When their mistakes coincide, being right together is the same 80%.

prompt: How many of the seventy cases did the majority of `v3-examples`, `v4-only-json` and `v6-escaped` get right?
hint: The `majority of 3` line.

prompt: Two of the prompts score 56 of 70. Why does their majority with the third reach only 58 rather than the 63 the arithmetic promises?
hint: Look at the cases all three got wrong.

choices.text: `pl vote` throws away the third prompt's ballots
choices.why: Every reply that parses casts a ballot.

choices.text: Their mistakes fall on the same cases
choices.why: Right: eleven cases wrong under all three, where independent voters would put half a case.

choices.text: Seventy cases are too few for a vote
choices.why: The size of the set does not change what a vote does on each case.

choices.text: The third prompt is so much worse than the other two that it drags the majority down
choices.why: 53 against 56 is close, and every case it alone got wrong was outvoted.

prompt: In the `uniq -c` count, how many cases were wrong under all three prompts?
hint: Count the lines that begin with 3.

prompt: Ten cases were wrong under exactly one of the three prompts. What did the vote do with them?
hint: Two against one.

choices.text: Kept the wrong answer whenever it came from `v3-examples`, the most expensive prompt
choices.why: Cost plays no part in a vote.

choices.text: Fixed all ten
choices.why: Right: the other two outvoted the one that was wrong.

choices.text: Settled them as ties
choices.why: Two against one is not a tie.

choices.text: Fixed only the ones that parsed
choices.why: A reply that does not parse casts no ballot, so the other two decide.

prompt: In `pl vote`, a reply that does not parse casts no ___, and the other replies decide the case.
hint: What a voter puts in the box.

prompt: You want an ensemble whose members make different mistakes. Which of these is the weakest way to get that?
hint: Where would a shared blind spot survive?

choices.text: Using a different model for one member
choices.why: A different model has different gaps, which is what you want.

choices.text: Giving one member evidence the others lack, such as definitions of the categories
choices.why: Different evidence changes what the member knows.

choices.text: Three rewordings of one prompt to one model
choices.why: Right: what the model does not know, it does not know under any wording.

choices.text: Having one member reach the answer a different way
choices.why: A different route makes different slips.

prompt: Five samples per message at temperature 0.8, voted. How many of the seventy did the vote get right?
hint: The `majority of the samples` line.

prompt: In the stand-in, why can a vote of samples at 0.8 not beat the single answer at temperature 0, apart from ties?
hint: What is each sample, relative to the temperature-0 answer?

choices.text: Samples at 0.8 are not valid JSON
choices.why: Almost all of them parse.

choices.text: Five samples is too few, and fifty would beat temperature 0 comfortably
choices.why: More samples get closer to the temperature-0 answer, not past it.

choices.text: At best it finds the temperature-0 label
choices.why: Right: sampling adds errors around it and voting removes some of them.

choices.text: The stand-in ignores temperature
choices.why: `t37` got two different wrong labels in two samples.

prompt: A report says the vote of five samples beat a single sample at 0.8, 52 of 70 against about 65%. What is wrong with the comparison?
hint: What else could you have run instead?

choices.text: Nothing; the vote is better
choices.why: Better than its own member, worse than the temperature-0 call.

choices.text: It is measured against a member
choices.why: Right: against temperature 0, which got 56, the vote loses.

choices.text: The percentages use different denominators
choices.why: Converting both to percentages fixes that; the problem is what is being compared.

choices.text: A vote should be run at temperature 1
choices.why: A higher temperature adds more errors for the vote to remove.

prompt: Wang and others (2022) reported gains from self-consistency. What kind of task were they on, and why does that matter here?
hint: How many routes lead to a one-word label?

choices.text: Reasoning with many paths to one answer; a label has one path
choices.why: Right: wrong chains scatter, right ones converge, and a classification has no chain.

choices.text: Classification of customer messages, the same as here
choices.why: The paper was about reasoning problems such as arithmetic.

choices.text: Translation, where samples differ only in style
choices.why: Translation is not what the paper measured.

choices.text: Tasks run at temperature 0
choices.why: At temperature 0 every sample would be the same.

prompt: How does `pl vote` settle a tie between labels?
hint: Six of the sampled votes were ties.

choices.text: It calls the model once more
choices.why: It makes no new calls.

choices.text: It counts the case as wrong
choices.why: A tie still has a winner.

choices.text: It picks the label listed first in the prompt
choices.why: That is a rule of the stand-in's own scoring, not of the vote.

choices.text: It takes the first sample's answer
choices.why: Right: with several runs, the first run's.

prompt: Per million messages, the three members cost 127,749, 85,084 and 92,649 cents. How many times the cost of `v6-escaped` alone is the ensemble? One decimal place.
hint: Add them and divide by 92,649.

prompt: An ensemble's three calls run at the same time. What is the wait for an answer?
hint: They are independent of each other.

choices.text: The sum of the three latencies
choices.why: That is the wait if they run one after another.

choices.text: The slowest member's
choices.why: Right: the money is the sum, the wait is not.

choices.text: The fastest member's, because the first answer to arrive is used straight away
choices.why: A vote needs all the ballots.

choices.text: The average of the three
choices.why: Nothing finishes until the slowest does.

prompt: Which of these make an ensemble more likely to be worth what it costs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things, each measurable.

choices.text: A wrong answer is expensive
choices.why: Yes: two answers in seventy can be worth a lot.

choices.text: Each call is cheap
choices.why: Yes: the bill is n times a small number.

choices.text: The members make different mistakes
choices.why: Yes: that is the condition the arithmetic needs.

choices.text: The members are rewordings of the same prompt
choices.why: That is the case where their mistakes coincide.

prompt: Put these in order of how many of the seventy cases they got right, fewest first.
items: The vote of five samples at 0.8

prompt: Match each observation from this lesson to what explains it.
hint: One explanation each.

pairs.left: Eleven cases wrong under all three prompts
Ten cases wrong under one prompt, all fixed
The vote of samples below temperature 0
pairs.right: Errors added around the favoured label

pairs.left: Five samples costing five times as much

prompt: A team votes five samples at temperature 1 and reports 85% against 75% for a single sample. Before adopting it, what do you ask for?
hint: What is the best single call, and what does the vote cost?

choices.text: The same comparison at temperature 2
choices.why: More randomness gives the vote more to undo.

choices.text: A vote of ten samples instead of five
choices.why: That still compares the vote with its own members.

choices.text: Nothing more: ten points is a large gain
choices.why: Ten points over a sample, not over the best single call.

choices.text: Its baseline at 0, and its price
choices.why: Right: that is the comparison that decides, and the price of winning it.
